title: Desportes
html:
Thibault Desportes, secretary to the Duke of Mayenne.

Desportes' letters to Pietro Aldobrandini (nephew of Pope Clement VIII) and Girolamo Frachetta (Mayenne's informant and trusted man in Rome) attempt to explain and defend Mayenne's actions to the Pope in the wake of French king Henry IV's anticipated conversion to Catholicism.
body:
[Thibault Desportes](https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/girolamo-frachetta_(Dizionario-Biografico)/.), secretary to the [Duke of Mayenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Mayenne).

Desportes' letters to [Pietro Aldobrandini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Aldobrandini) (nephew of [Pope Clement VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VIII)) and [Girolamo Frachetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girolamo_Frachetta) (Mayenne's informant and trusted man in Rome) attempt to explain and defend Mayenne's actions to the Pope in the wake of French king [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France)'s anticipated conversion to Catholicism.

title: Pietro Aldobrandini
html: (1571 - 1621) - nephew of Pope Clement VIII. Aldobrandini handled France, Spain and Savoy in the papal secretariat. Merely 22 years of age when Desportes' letters were written, Aldobrandini was elevated by Clement VIII to Cardinal two months later, in September 1593.
body: (1571 - 1621) - nephew of Pope Clement VIII.  Aldobrandini handled France, Spain and Savoy in the papal secretariat.  Merely 22 years of age when Desportes' letters were written, Aldobrandini was elevated by Clement VIII to Cardinal two months later, in September 1593.

title: our destruction seems inevitable
html: Henry IV announced his plan to convert to Catholicism in May 1593. Desportes believes that Henry IV's conversion will force Mayenne to sign a truce with Henry IV, which will eventually lead to the end of the Catholic League's campaign against him.
body: Henry IV announced his plan to [convert to Catholicism](https://catholicunderthehood.com/2010/07/25/today-in-catholic-history-henry-iv-becomes-catholic/) in May 1593.  Desportes believes that Henry IV's conversion will force Mayenne to sign a truce with Henry IV, which will eventually lead to the end of the Catholic League's campaign against him.

title: could not fail to cause His Holiness extreme displeasure
titleHtml: could not fail to cause His Holiness extreme displeasure
html: In this letter, Desportes underscores the official state of affairs pursuant to which Mayenne and the Pope were allies in the Catholic League opposed to Henry IV. As Desportes seems to have understood, the reality was quite different: while Clement VIII initially supported the Catholic League's war against Henry IV (as did the previous Popes), Henry's growing strength and later conversion to Catholicism made a reconciliation possible between himself and the Vatican. In September 1595, just over two years since Henry IV's conversion, Clement VIII lifted Henry's excommunication from the Church.

title: Thus I had resolved to write no more to him or to Your Most Illustrious Lordship
titleHtml: Thus I had resolved to write no more to him or to Your Most Illustrious Lordship
html: The Vatican had not heard any news from Desportes in at least two months. In his letter, Desportes explains that this was because he did not want to deliver the bad news (i.e., news of Henry IV's increasing strength and impending conversion) to Clement VIII. In the Frachetta letter, Desportes is more frank, questioning whether Mayenne "could hold out in the long run" against Henry IV given that the tides had turned against him.

title: in this kingdom
html: i.e., France. At the time when these letters are written, Mayenne continues to hold Paris. Henry IV's conversion was designed, at least in part, to help him win the capital - hence his famous declaration that "Paris is well worthy of a Mass." In fact, Henry had to wait for many months after his conversion to enter Paris, which did not open its gates to him until March 1594.

title: Monsieur Mateouci
html:
(elsewhere, Mateuci) - Girolamo Matteucci (1544 - 1609). In April 1591, Matteucci was appointed by Pope Gregory XIV as the commander of the papal forces sent to France to join the fight against Henry IV. This army experienced various issues with provisioning and payment and did not manage to arrive until mid-September 1591; two months later, following the death of Pope Gregory, it nearly disbanded. Even in this short time, Mayenne attempted - unsuccessfully - both to have Matteucci assassinated and kidnapped.

Despite these troubles and Clement VIII's increasing unease with providing further support to the war against Henry IV, Matteucci continued the campaign and even personally engaged an additional German regiment for the war - which angered the Vatican. In a letter of September 7, 1592, Matteucci was ordered to stop spending money on troops as his personal initiative; shortly thereafter, he was replaced by Innocenzo Malvasia as commander of the papal troops in France and returned to Italy.

(elsewhere, Mateuci) - [Girolamo Matteucci](https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/girolamo-matteucci_(Dizionario-Biografico)/) (1544 - 1609).  In April 1591, Matteucci was appointed  by Pope Gregory XIV as the commander of the papal forces sent to France to join the fight against Henry IV.  This army experienced various issues with provisioning and payment and did not manage to arrive until mid-September 1591; two months later, following the death of Pope Gregory, it nearly disbanded.  Even in this short time, Mayenne attempted - unsuccessfully - both to have Matteucci assassinated and kidnapped.  

Despite these troubles and Clement VIII's increasing unease with providing further support to the war against Henry IV, Matteucci continued the campaign and even personally engaged an additional German regiment for the war - which angered the Vatican.  In a letter of September 7, 1592, Matteucci was ordered to stop spending money on troops as his personal initiative; shortly thereafter, he was replaced by Innocenzo Malvasia as commander of the papal troops in France and returned to Italy.

title: Monsieur de Malvoisie
html: Innocenzo Malvasia (1552 - 1612). Malvasia took over the commission of the papal army in France from Girloamo Matteucci in December 1592. He dismissed these troops in early 1593, causing Mayenne to send an angry letter to Clement VIII remonstrating Malvasia for doing so and also complaining that Malvasia had refused to acknowledge Mayenne's authority and declared that he would obey only Charles de Lorraine, Duke of Guise (the candidate for the Infanta's hand proposed by Philip II of Spain).

title: the legate
html: Filippo Sega, Cardinal of Piacenza (1537 - 1596), who became Clement VIII's legate in 1592. Sega favored the Spanish interests in the Catholic League's war against Henry IV, which was directly contrary to Mayenne's interests. He is portrayed as the archvillain in Desportes letters: "our friends have shown themselves not merely neutral, but outright enemies" is clearly a reference to Sega. In his letter to Pietro Aldobrandini, Desportes asks that future communications between Mayenne and Clement VIII be direct instead of going through Sega.

title: proceed to the election of a king
titleHtml: proceed to the election of a king
html: The Catholic League's chosen successor to the French throne was Infanta Isabella Clara Eugenia, daughter of Philip II of Spain. Under existing succession laws, Isabella was permitted to ascend the throne so long as she was married to a suitable husband. Philip II lobbied for several candidates for Isabella's husband, eventually settling on Charles of Lorraine, Duke of Guise. Mayenne blocked Charles' election as king and proposed the candidacy of his own son to marry Isabella.

title: we would need many deeds before we could be made to reject the prospect of peace.  It will be no small achievement if we temper it into a truce
titleHtml: we would need many deeds before we could be made to reject the prospect of peace.  It will be no small achievement if we temper it into a truce
html:
Mayenne is desperate to continue the war against Henry IV, but now finds himself increasingly bereft of allies and resources - especially with Henry IV's conversion to Catholicism looming. Desportes indicates that Mayenne will do what he can to ensure that no permanent peace agreement is signed between the parties, but seemingly has no choice but to agree to a truce.

The truce between Henry IV and Mayenne was signed on July 31, 1593, less than a week after Henry IV's conversion. In 1594, Paris opened its gates to Henry IV, forcing Mayenne to retreat. Mayenne finally submitted to Henry IV's rule in September 1595, was given a substantial gift by the French king, and wound up fighting alongside him against the Spanish at Amiens in 1597.

The truce between Henry IV and Mayenne was signed on July 31, 1593, less than a week after Henry IV's conversion.  In 1594, Paris opened its gates to Henry IV, forcing Mayenne to retreat.  Mayenne finally submitted to Henry IV's rule in September 1595, was given a substantial gift by the French king, and wound up fighting alongside him against the Spanish at Amiens in 1597.

title: they offer to show letters from Your Most Illustrious Lordship
titleHtml: they offer to show letters from Your Most Illustrious Lordship
html:
According to Desportes, Henry IV is in possession of letters from the Vatican confirming that Henry IV's excommunication will be lifted if he converts to Catholicism.

In fact, it took more than two years following Henry IV's conversion for his excommunication to be lifted (in September 1595).

title: Pope Gregory
html: Pope Gregory XIV (1535 - 1591). Gregory XIV enthusiastically financed and otherwise supported the Catholic League in its struggle against Henry IV, although he began favoring Spanish interests over the French in this war. Desportes is happy to forget these past issues when he reminds the Vatican regarding the financial support that Paris had received from Gregory XIV.

title: Mayenne
html: Charles de Lorraine, Duke of Mayenne (1554 - 1611). Mayenne took charge of the Catholic League after his brother Henri de Guise was killed in 1588. Mayenne's position depended on keeping together a coalition opposed to Henry IV while at the same time retaining influence over the coalition's choice of a Catholic successor to the French throne. Mayenne staunchly opposed the installation of a Spanish monarch onto the French throne. Desportes is Mayenne's secretary. In these two letters, he conveys the state of affairs in the light most favorable to Mayenne.
